issues.legal_issue: An order directing the sale of property in a statutory financial-corporation proceeding is appealable to the High Court when the governing procedure incorporates the Code of Civil Procedure’s execution-sale procedure.
material_facts: A company had mortgaged its property as security for a loan from a financial corporation.
A District Judge ordered the mortgaged property sold under the statutory procedure.
After the sale, the company applied to set it aside; the District Judge refused, and the High Court dismissed the company’s appeal on the ground that no appeal lay.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in holding that no appeal lay. The Code of Civil Procedure’s provision for an appeal from an order refusing to set aside an execution sale applied through the statutory incorporation of that Code’s procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(8) of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, provides that an attachment or sale order is to be carried into effect, as far as practicable, in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, for attachment or sale in execution of a decree. “Manner” includes the method of procedure, including an appeal. An order refusing to set aside an execution sale is appealable under Order XLIII, Rule 1(j), of the Code. Section 32(9), which expressly provides an appeal for orders under subsections (5) and (7), does not exclude an appeal in this distinct procedural setting; no earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.statutory_property_sale_proceeding: The proceeding concerned the sale of secured property under a statutory financial-corporation process.
predicates.execution_sale_procedure_incorporated: The governing process required the sale to be carried out, so far as practicable, using the procedure for execution sales.
predicates.related_execution_sale_order_appealable: The corresponding order in an execution sale could be appealed under the applicable civil procedure.

issues.definition: When a statutory secured-property sale uses execution-sale procedure and the corresponding execution-sale order is appealable, an appeal lies to the High Court.

issues.legal_issue: A District Judge exercising statutory functions is not a persona designata when the statute permits those functions to be exercised by other judges or courts.
material_facts: The sale proceeding was heard by a District Judge exercising functions under the statutory scheme.
The statute provided that those functions could also be exercised by a judge of a city civil court, the High Court in specified circumstances, or an additional District Judge.
issues.conclusion: The Act did not confer jurisdiction on the District Judge as a persona designata.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(11) of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, provided for the functions of a District Judge under the section to be exercised by specified other judicial officers or courts. That allocation shows that the authority is attached to a judicial office or court and not to a particular person designated individually; no earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.statutory_judicial_proceeding: The matter was a statutory proceeding assigned to a District Judge in a judicial capacity.
predicates.statutory_function_transferable_among_ju: The governing scheme allowed the same function to be exercised by other judges or courts.

issues.definition: When a statutory judicial function can be exercised by different judges or courts, the assigned judge does not act as a persona designata.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal challenging the refusal to set aside a sale should not be dismissed summarily when the record presents matters potentially supporting a challenge to the sale.
material_facts: The company appealed the refusal to set aside the sale of its property.
The sale had been preceded by repeated sale attempts, and no public notice was given of an adjournment.
An expert valuation obtained during the sale process was substantially higher than the eventual sale price, and the company had protested the valuation process.
The High Court dismissed the appeal summarily, stating that it found no substance on the merits.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in dismissing the appeal summarily. The Supreme Court set aside that dismissal and remanded the appeal for disposal according to law, without deciding the merits of the challenge to the sale.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered that there was prima facie something to be said on the merits of the challenge to the District Judge’s refusal to set aside the sale. It therefore held that summary dismissal was unjustified on these facts; no statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this conclusion.

rule.if: appeal_from_refusal_to_set_aside_sale and sale_process_irregularities_present and sale_price_below_assessed_value and appellate_court_dismissed_without_full_consideration

predicates.appeal_from_refusal_to_set_aside_sale: The proceeding was an appeal from a refusal to set aside an auction sale.
predicates.sale_process_irregularities_present: The sale process included a procedural concern, such as an adjournment without public notice.
predicates.sale_price_below_assessed_value: The property was sold for less than an assessment obtained during the sale process.
predicates.appellate_court_dismissed_without_full_c: The appellate court rejected the appeal summarily without full consideration of the challenge.

issues.definition: When an appeal from refusal to set aside a sale presents procedural concerns and a sale price below an assessment, summary rejection without full consideration is unjustified.
